newsitem.title: FRANCE: Workers stage Euro-demo over Renault job cuts.
newsitem.headline: Workers stage Euro-demo over Renault job cuts.

text.p: Thousands of European car workers marched in Paris on Tuesday to protest against plans by carmaker Renault to close an assembly plant in Belgium and cut nearly 3,000 jobs in France this year.
But Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer stuck to his plans to close the plant and cut the European work force of the carmaker, which is expected to report huge losses next week.
He also received support from French Industry Minister Franck Borotra, who said the company's survival was at stake.

Union leaders said Schweitzer merely repeated at a European works council meeting after the protest the reasons for the tough measures. "It was a big disappointment," said Jean-Paul Verbeke, a delegate from the Belgian union CSC.

The council authorised its secretary to take legal action against Renault for allegedly breaching French and European directives in announcing the closure of the Vilvoorde plant, which employs 3,100 people.
Schweitzer said the company had complied fully with Belgian law and European directives in announcing the closure.
The council did not decide whether to begin court action, "but if we asked for a mandate, there's a strong probability we will," said Daniel Richter, a spokesman for the CFDT union.

The unions said between 10,000 and 12,000 people, mostly from France and Belgium with a handful from Spain, marched from Renault's headquarters to the site of the works council meeting near the Eiffel Tower. Police put the figure closer to 7,000.

Some 3,000 workers and relatives travelled from Vilvoorde. They were joined by about 50 workers from Spain, where the government halted a $14 million modernisation subsidy after Renault's job-cutting measures provoked an outcry.
"This pan-European demonstration is a first at Renault," said Philippe Martinez, a spokesman for the Communist-led CGT union, the biggest at the company.
"The unions are taking the initiative to create a Europe of social standards," said Emmanuel Couvreur of the CFDT.
"Europe's politicians cannot be relied upon to move things forward socially. Only the European unions can provide a counterweight to free-marketeering excesses," he said.
Unions have called for more labour action on Thursday, when Renault is expected to detail plans to cut 2,764 jobs in France this year to the French works council.
Renault has drawn sharp criticism over the Belgian plant closure. Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene condemned the move and President Jacques Chirac said it was poorly handled.
But Schweitzer received support on Tuesday from Borotra, who said Renault's survival hung in the balance.
"You talk about a strategy of job-cutting. The strategy at stake here is the strategy of survival for the company," Borotra said in response to a parliamentary questioner.

He accused the European Commission of double standards. "When JVC relocated out of Lorraine, when Hoover pulled out of Burgundy, when Grundig closed down its Creutzwald activities, I don't recall getting support from the European Commission," Borotra said, citing closures in France in the last five years.
"Workers are worried, and I too am worried about the future of the European car industry," the industry minister said.

The outlook is grim, with quotas limiting Japanese car imports ending in 2000. Korean carmakers are also making rapid inroads in the slow-growing market, plagued by overcapacity estimated at 20 percent or more.

Renault, the smallest and weakest of Europe's six carmakers, is expected to report an operating loss of more than two billion francs ($350 million) for 1996 and a total loss of close to six billion francs including restructuring charges.
